title: Jeremiah 17:12–18
context: Jeremiah speaks in prayer. He praises the LORD's glorious throne and sanctuary and calls the LORD the hope of Israel and the spring of living waters, an image also found in 2:13. He asks for healing and salvation, protests that he has not desired the day of disaster, and asks the LORD to be his refuge and to bring the promised judgment on his persecutors. This is one of several personal prayers of Jeremiah in the book, often grouped with 11:18–20, 15:15–21, and 20:7–18.

verses.text: A glorious throne, set on high from the beginning, is the place of our sanctuary.
verses.arminianNotes: "A glorious throne, set on high from the beginning, is the place of our sanctuary." Arminian readers see Jeremiah turning from judgment to worship, finding security in the LORD's throne.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the sanctuary is the place of the LORD's glorious throne. Jeremiah's confidence rests in God's reign, not in the temple as a building, which he elsewhere warns against trusting.

verses.text: LORD, the hope of Israel, all who forsake you will be disappointed. Those who depart from me will be written in the earth, because they have forsaken the LORD, the spring of living waters.
verses.arminianNotes: "LORD, the hope of Israel, all who forsake you will be disappointed." Arminian readers see that turning from the LORD leads to shame, since the people have "forsaken the LORD, the spring of living waters."
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the parallel with 2:13, where the people have forsaken "the spring of living waters." Those who depart "will be written in the earth," a likely image of names that fade.

verses.text: Heal me, O LORD, and I will be healed. Save me, and I will be saved; for you are my praise.
verses.arminianNotes: "Heal me, O LORD, and I will be healed." Arminian readers see Jeremiah's personal trust: only the LORD can truly heal and save, and the prophet asks for that help.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the strong confidence: "Save me, and I will be saved." Salvation and healing are the LORD's work alone. Both traditions treat this prayer as shared ground.

verses.text: Behold, they ask me, “Where is the LORD’s word? Let it be fulfilled now.”
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah reports that the people ask, "Where is the LORD’s word?" Arminian readers see Jeremiah mocked by people who doubt that his warnings will come true and dare the LORD to act.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the people's taunt, "Let it be fulfilled now," shows how they mistake delay for emptiness. Jeremiah brings their mockery to the LORD in prayer.

verses.text: As for me, I have not hurried from being a shepherd after you. I haven’t desired the woeful day. You know. That which came out of my lips was before your face.
verses.arminianNotes: "As for me, I have not hurried from being a shepherd after you." Arminian readers see Jeremiah defending his faithfulness: he has not run from his calling nor "desired the woeful day."
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Jeremiah appeals to God's knowledge: "You know." His words were spoken before God's face. He takes no pleasure in the judgment he must announce.

verses.text: Don’t be a terror to me. You are my refuge in the day of evil.
verses.arminianNotes: "Don’t be a terror to me. You are my refuge in the day of evil." Arminian readers see the prophet asking that the LORD, his refuge, not become a source of fear to him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the tension in Jeremiah's prayer: the God he serves is his refuge, yet his calling brings him great distress. Both traditions value the honesty of this prayer.

verses.text: Let them be disappointed who persecute me, but don’t let me be disappointed. Let them be dismayed, but don’t let me be dismayed. Bring on them the day of evil, and destroy them with double destruction.
verses.arminianNotes: "Let them be disappointed who persecute me." Arminian readers see Jeremiah asking God to vindicate him and bring the announced judgment on those who reject his message.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Jeremiah's request echoes the LORD's own threatened judgment. They compare Jeremiah 15:15, "avenge me of my persecutors," and read the prayer as appealing to God's justice rather than personal revenge.
